Mr. Speaker, the idea of making water pollution a criminal offence is an excellent one provided we first solve the problem of anonymous, mass pollution by municipalities. Unless we do this first such a law would merely make it a criminal offence to flush a toilet and would be unenforceable.
The question of pollution is a most vital one in my constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle where 100,000 people dump their untreated sewage into beautiful lake St. Louis every day. All the towns concerned would like to do something about it but unfortunately as the treatment of sewage by any one town only benefits the towns immediately downstream and not the town itself it is difficult to persuade taxpayers to approve the high cost of installing disposal plants. Most municipalities are ready to pay their share of the cost of such projects but feel that the cost of this expensive work should be also shared by the dominion and provincial governments. The province of Quebec has already set aside $250,000 to study the question on a province-wide basis but in our county we do not need any further research to convince us that a repulsive and dangerous condition exists.
Last December, as mayor of the city of Dorval, I called a meeting of the mayors, managers and engineers of the 18 municipalities that make up my constituency. They were unanimous in forming a non-political, technical planning board to co-operate in the study and planning of the most economic way of solving this most urgent problem. However, the municipalities feel, and rightly so, that the initiative must come from the higher levels of government in co-operation, and the problem of water pollution should therefore occupy a position of high priority in any federal-provincial conference.

To make individual pollution a criminal offence will be an excellent move, particularly when we have solved the question of mass pollution in the first place.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PUNISHMENT FOR WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say just a few words on this resolution that the government should give consideration to amending the Criminal Code so that appropriate punishment be visited upon those responsible for water pollution. I cannot speak from the legal point of view, the medical point of view or the engineering point of view, but I can speak as a Canadian well aware of and proud of the beauties of Canada. I think there is in this debate sweet harmony or complete unanimity in which to wipe out the pollution of our beautiful lakes and rivers. All of us want to maintain, or perhaps more properly recapture the uncontaminated purity of our waterways.
Recently there was a newspaper story which I found rather shocking in its disclosure of a situation in Brockville. The Brockville people had been warned that their water was unsafe. The article said:
An analysis of Brockville's water supply over an extended period of time showed intermittent heavy bacterial pollution much in excess of recognized standards.
Under existing conditions I suppose that could happen in any of our constituencies, because this was caused by pollution from various outlets and drainage in and around Brockville. In my riding of York-Humber, the Humber is a lovely, winding little river which goes all through the riding and which has been spoiled by pollution. I was just reading tonight that nearly one-fifth of the total metropolitan area of Toronto lies within the Humber watershed. It is one of the main drainages for urban waste. The low flows from the Humber in summer do not provide sufficient dilution for those wastes and a serious pollution problem exists.
I suppose we must blame progress for the despoiling of our waterways; but it seems to me that now the ingenuity of man must find a detour in the path of progress, a detour to correct the wrong that is being done. To make this detour is going to cost money. I believe it is the responsibility of all levels of government and, as the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) said this afternoon, it is also the responsibility of industry. In Ontario, however, it is estimated that the cost of cleaning up our rivers could be as high as a billion dollars within the next decade or so.
In this debate hon. members have said the resolution of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson) may be rather drastic, a sort of shock treatment, and perhaps that is so; but it seems to me that the dumping of

sewage in our beautiful rivers is downright barbaric. It must be corrected and I believe that all levels of government must tackle the problem. Certainly, water pollution, as has been proved throughout this debate today, has a very definite bearing on human welfare and on human health. So, too, has pollution of the air we breathe. This is found to be more of a problem in my city riding of York-Humber. I am sorry that the hon. member for Selkirk did not include appropriate punishment for the offence of air pollution as well.
In my riding of York-Humber, and I suppose this is true of any city riding, pollution of the air we breathe is an increasing problem. The greatest smoke nuisance in my riding is created by a railway roundhouse.
I suppose in the years ahead-I hope very immediately ahead-the replacement of the old steam engines by diesel engines will remove this nuisance, but in the meantime I do marvel at the tolerance of the people who have to live within that air pollution. Before you stop me, Mr. Speaker, from jumping from water to air, I want to say that we have this air pollution or smoke pollution or water pollution. The time has come when all citizens must tackle the problem and for that reason I welcome and warmly support this resolution of the hon. member for Selkirk.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising after hon. members who have dealt with the question of water pollution in a masterly way, with a wealth of supporting evidence, it will be very difficult indeed, for me, especially in this, my maiden speech, to make a new and very definite contribution to this debate.
However, because it is an important problem, I did not want to miss my chance of congratulating the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson) for bringing before the house a problem which is becoming increasingly serious with the growing development and industrialization of this country.
The fact of the matter is that today water pollution is affecting more and more areas of Canada. As an Ottawa valley resident, I know that for several years now the pollution of the Ottawa river has been a very serious problem. What I did not realize is that the problem is so acute in every area of the country, especially in circumstances such as those mentioned by the hon. member for Selkirk.
He, in fact, spoke of a river in his district, the Red river, which I knew only by name and through old songs that lumbermen and some of our pioneers, more particularly the early settlers in my own constituency of
Criminal Code
Pontiac-Timiskaming, used to sing. I was therefore quite surprised to learn that this river, which to my mind seemed full of poetic charm and magic attractions, was polluted to the extent where it constituted a serious threat in that area.
I wonder however if the remedy proposed by the hon. member for Selkirk would really solve the problem.
Before amending the Criminal Code, we should study the question thoroughly in order to avert a possible clash of jurisdictions. A number of provinces have, in fact, already adopted legislation which, in certain specified cases, prohibit water pollution. I wonder if this parliament would have jurisdiction in this connection. Another thing which we should consider is that nobody, wilfully or maliciously, would really wish to contribute to the pollution of waters. If there is water pollution, Mr. Speaker, it is not because people want to break the law governing public health. It has merely been brought about through the force of circumstances. Our country has been developing at a very rapid rate over the past few years and we are undergoing what are commonly called growing pains, among which we must include sewage disposal.
If this parliament were to adopt legislation which would make water pollution a criminal offence, what could we do, since, up to now, we have taken no adequate action to change the situation? If we were to amend the Criminal Code to make water pollution a criminal offence, we would perforce be turning into criminals a great many law abiding citizens.
Mr. Speaker, just as did previous speakers, I submit that, before we proceed to amend our Criminal Code, we should call a federal-provincial conference which would include representatives of municipalities so that the authorities concerned may act together in seeking means to solve this problem which is becoming a real plague. This conference could set up a permanent controlling agency, whose duty would be to study all aspects of the matter.
Mr. Speaker, I heartily commend the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). He brilliantly stated the case and ably went into the most technical aspects of water pollution.
After such a complete and comprehensive speech, I find it very difficult to deal with the matter. However, I do wish to say that in my view this discussion was most useful and that it will certainly cause not only in

Criminal Code
this house but in the public and among other authorities, a favourable reaction which will stimulate the search for a solution to this serious problem. I am convinced that, with the modern technology and methods that we have had for the past few years, we will manage to put an end to this situation.
This problem interests me all the more because it affects the Ottawa river, which rises in the pellucid streams of the mountains and remote areas of my constituency. It is certainly too bad that on reaching the national capital, this water should be so polluted instead of being improved, as it were, by the presence of so many luminaries in this house. I therefore hope that the house will be able to find the means of putting an end to this problem.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PUNISHMENT FOR WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleague from Pontiac-Timiskaming (Mr. Martineau), I represent a riding where unfortunately, despite the enchanting spectacle of Beloeil mountain mirrored in the magnificent Richelieu river, I, too, must recognize the existence of a water pollution problem concerning that river. It is not however peculiar to this river, for the Richelieu is not the only one to be polluted. I would like, therefore very frankly and very simply, to state my views on this matter.
Water pollution has become a very important problem because it has increased with industrial progress and the development of heavily populated urban areas. It is now a technical matter of administrative concern.
I need only state, as an example, the fact that the public health act of the province of Quebec controls to a certain extent, problems relating to water pollution. Section 40 of the Quebec public health act, chapter 183 of the Revised Statutes of the province of Quebec, 1941, states:
40.	Every camp used as a habitation for the workmen engaged in forest or mining operations or in roadwork must be erected in accordance with specimen plans supplied by the Provincial Bureau of Health.
It is a responsibility of that bureau to enact regulations to protect water against pollution. Now, here is section 41:
41.	Whenever an infringement of the preceding section or of the provincial health regulations respecting the sanitary condition of camps contemplated by paragraph 7 of section 8 is established to the satisfaction of the minister, he must give the offenders, the limit-holders, the mine-owners or the road-contractors, as the case may be, written notice to remedy the existing conditions forthwith, granting them a delay of fifteen days to do so.

If, after a delay of fifteen days, the sanitary conditions have not been rectified to his satisfaction, the minister may order and proceed to the suppression of such camps as human habitations and take the necessary legal proceedings against the limit-holders, the mine-owners or the road-contractors, operating themselves or through others, and they shall be held responsible for such infringement and shall be liable to a fine of not more than fifty dollars for each day during which such default continues.
Then, section 56 of that same chapter deals with drainage and with drinking-water. Section 56 states that:
No municipality shall establish or allow to be established, no corporation, company or person shall establish a water works or intake for drinking water or any device for the purification of water before submitting the plans and specifications prepared by a graduate engineer to the minister, and obtaining his approval.
In addition to the penalty attached to the infringement of this section, every work done without such previous approval shall be altered or demolished by the municipality, the corporation, firm or person doing the same, if the minister be of opinion that the water supplied may be injurious to health.
The Minister may require an analysis of the water to be made at the expense of the municipality, corporation, firm or person submitting the plans, before giving his approval.
No connection may be made between the public water distributing conduit and the distributing conduit of a private system, until the plans and specifications have been submitted to the minister and his approval has been obtained.
Plans and specifications of connections existing on the 13th of April 1933, were to be submitted to the Provincial Bureau of Health before the 1st of January 1934. Such connections must be done away with or altered, whenever, in the minister's opinion, they constitute a menace to public health. t This section shall apply also to proposed extensions of old installations.
And section 57 of the same act, concerning approval of drainage plans, provides as follows:
No municipality shall take or allow any steps to be taken and no corporation, company or person shall take any steps to carry out public or private drainage works or the installation of any plant for the treatment of sewage.
In addition to the penalty attached to the infringement of this section, every work done without such previous approval shall be altered or demolished by the municipality, the corporation, firm or person doing the same if the minister be of the opinion that the water supplied may be injurious to health.
This section shall apply also to proposed extensions of old installations.
58. The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may by regulation determine what must be shown by the plans and specifications submitted to the minister for approval under sections 56 and 57.
To the sections I have just quoted, section 59 adds:
No municipal by-law relating to the construction of waterworks, a filter, or any other plant for the treatment of water, to a sewage-system or any plants for the treatment of sewage, shall be submitted for the approval of the ratepayers, in case

such approval is required, before the plans and specifications of the works referred to in such bylaw, prepared by a graduate engineer, have been approved by the minister.
And section 60 adds the following provision:
Every infringement of sections 56, 57, 58 or 59 shall render the municipality, corporation, firm or person guilty thereof liable to a fine of not more than one hundred dollars.
There is also clause 61, which covers any case of collective, inexistent or insufficient service. It also deals with the extensive powers conferred upon the Public Services Board.
Clause 65 deals with polluted intake of water, and I quote:
Whenever the minister finds, after investigation, that the source of the water supply of any municipality or community in this province has been rendered impure by reason of the discharge of sewage or other waste matter, or whenever he finds, after investigation, that any stream, lake or pond has been rendered so impure as to give off foul or noxious odours injurious to the health or comfort of those living in the vicinity, it shall be the duty of such minister to communicate the results of his investigation to any municipality, corporation, or person responsible for such pollution and impurity. If, after having heard the parties interested, the minister considers that it is necessary to make any change or improvement, his duty shall be to call upon such municipality, corporation or person responsible to take the necessary steps to do away with the causes of such pollution or impurity. The work necessary to that end must be completed within a delay to be fixed by the minister.
Section 66 supplements the provisions of section 65:
Whenever the minister finds, after investigation, that the water supply of any municipality is impure and dangerous to health and that it is practically impossible to sufficiently improve the quality of such supply by removing the source or sources of pollution affecting it, or whenever said director finds, after investigation, that such water supply is being rendered impure by reason of the improper construction or inadequate size of existing water purification works, he shall notify the municipality, corporation or person, owning or operating such water supply, of the results of his investigation.
If, after hearing the interested parties, the minister considers that improvements or changes are necessary and should be made, he shall call upon the municipality, corporation or person, owning or operating such water supply, to change the source of supply or to install and place in operation water purification works or devices, or to change existing water purification works. The work necessary to that end must be completed within a delay to be fixed by the minister.
All these quotations, Mr. Chairman, prove that at least as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, there is extensive and complete legislation covering all aspects of water pollution, and not only in the public hygiene act but also in the Water Course act, chapter 98, Revised Statutes of 1941, an act respecting the use of water-courses and the driving of timber.
Criminal Code
Section 51 of this act deals with certain offences and provides for certain penalties and the recovery of fines and damages from logging companies which do not protect our waters against pollution. Section 51, chapter 98, reads as follows:
Subject to any jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada in this respect, and to the provisions of any acts passed in the exercise of such jurisdiction, any person who throws into any river, stream, creek or brook, any bark, slabs, waste stuff or other refuse of any sawmill, or stump, root, shrub, tanbark or leached ashes, and allows the same to remain and to obstruct such a river, stream, creek or brook, shall incur a penalty of not more than twenty dollars nor less than twenty cents for each day during which such obstruction remains there, over and above all damages resulting therefrom.
Nevertheless, if the obstruction be caused without malicious intent, in good faith, or in the exercise of a right, the person causing the same shall not be liable to any fine or damages unless upon failure to remove the obstruction after notice and within a reasonable time.
This Water-Course Act, section 51, mentions the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada in respect of the criminal law, where it states:
Subject to any jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada in this respect . . .
Mr. Speaker, in spite of all these legislative provisions enacted by the provincial authorities, who enjoy prior jurisdiction in this matter of water pollution, the fact remains that it is an administrative and technical problem. Moreover, so to speak, it is a problem of public education. This means that the problems brought about by water pollution and the resulting damages must be brought to the attention of the public. The public must be brought to react and to work to the solution of this serious problem and to prevent its spread.
As for the rivers and lakes which would possibly concern several provinces, it would be well to promote an exchange of information between the provinces concerned so as to determine the best solution to the problems involved. In other words, we must put first things first.
To speak only of the province of Quebec, I could mention that an act was adopted in 1955 concerning water pollution, with the express purpose of allowing this problem to be studied as a whole in order that the technical and administrative recommendations might be made for its solution. I will quote here the preamble to the act respecting the pollution of water, chapter 11 of the Revised Statutes of Quebec, 4-5 Elizabeth II, 1955-56.

Criminal Code
Whereas the pollution of the water of rivers and lakes is a serious danger to public health;
Whereas it is expedient to make a careful study of this complicated problem and the means that can be taken to solve it;
Therefore, Her Majesty, with the advice and consent of the Legislative Council and of the Legislative Assembly of Quebec, enacts as follows:
1.	The Lieutenant-Governor in Council is authorized to form a committee of not more than five persons to study the problem of the pollution of the waters of the public domain of the Province.
He shall appoint the members of such committee one of whom he shall designate as chairman.
He may also appoint to assist them a secretary, technicians and any other persons whose services he may deem useful.
He shall determine the remuneration of the members of the committee and of the persons so appointed to assist them.
2.	The committee shall inquire into the extent, nature and causes of the present pollution of waters of the public domain, try to find out the remedies therefor, and the measures required to prevent further cases of pollution, and report its findings and suggestions to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.
3.	In the execution of its mandate and to facilitate the settlement of the problems deriving from the pollution of waters of the interprovincial public domain, the committee, under the direction of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, is authorized to collaborate with the other interested governmental authorities.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, instead of branding everybody as a criminal, we should, in my humble opinion, let the experts suggest scientific means of solving the problem. Any suggestion for amending the Criminal Code will bring no solution. I believe it might even be dangerous. This problem will exist as long as the experts who are studying it have not brought out constructive and truly practical recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, I think that most of the constituencies of our country are affected by this water pollution evil. Though I am not a lawyer, I must say that I fully share the views expressed by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson) when he said, among other things, that this problem is the concern of the provincial government as much as of the federal government.
I recognize that the federal government can enact measures setting penalties for those who pollute waters. However, this would not solve the problem. For years municipalities have been running their sewage into our rivers, and manufacturers have been dumping their waste products into our rivers. That is the main cause of water pollution.
Now then, municipal sewerage is a provincial responsibility while laws governing

manufactures in our provinces are of provincial jurisdiction. In fact, by quoting several statutes, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville clearly demonstrated that the provinces are specially concerned in this problem of water pollution.
I remember that when I sat on the Federal District Commission we studied this matter with respect to the area in which the commission is concerned. We found out that in 1953 the province of Ontario set up a committee whose particular duty was to study this matter and that in 1955 the province of Quebec also set up a commission whose duty was to co-operate with the province of Ontario in seeking a solution to the problem of water pollution. On this occasion, no request was made to the federal government except that it kindly give financial assistance to provinces and municipalities in preventing water pollution.
If this motion were to be adopted, I wonder where it would lead us to. Even if fines were imposed on manufacturers or municipalities, would it change the problem? For the city of Hull alone, $40 million would be required to divert water from sewers and elsewhere to a disposal plant. In the case of the city of Ottawa the cost would be over $100 million.
In the city of Montreal, sewer diversion would cost a fantastic sum. And if large industrial plants were requested to change their existing systems, there again the cost would run into millions.
There is not a single municipality in Canada which could undertake such works at its own expense, and I do not believe that provincial governments are in a position to bear the full cost of changes required by water pollution.
I feel that, instead of asking the federal government to write into our statutes and into our Criminal Code new rules which nobody will ever be able to enforce, it would be better to ask for the establishment of a commission representing the provinces and the federal government, with a view to finding the means of educating people, as was suggested some moments ago, and to change a situation which has lasted so long, that it cannot be eliminated overnight.
I know that in Gatineau Mills the International Paper Company has put up an alcohol plant which is making use of wood waste. This has been of help, and I believe that the International Paper Company, in

Gatineau Mills, is not polluting the water as much as the E. B. Eddy Company, because they are using their wood waste, while the E. B. Eddy Company is not. The same can be said for almost every paper mill along the Ottawa river; the wastes are dumped into the river, and that is what causes pollution.
Even the federal government is guilty. At its Chalk river plant, all the waste of the atomic plant is dumped into the nearby creek whence they eventually pass into the Ottawa river. We would therefore have to start by convicting the federal government for polluting the Ottawa river. This would be rather difficult to do. So I think that, instead of passing that resolution, which suggests that a penalty be imposed on everybody, it would be better to ask the federal and provincial governments to establish a board or commission which would inquire into the best ways to prevent water pollution not only in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, but all over the country.

Mr. Speaker, after all these outstanding speeches on the matter of water pollution, I do feel somewhat ill at ease, but I would nevertheless like to offer a few remarks. In my constituency a rather difficult situation arose some years ago. I would like to say a few words to the house in this regard. It concerns the Laflamme river and a situation which has been brought about by a producing mine in the Barraute area. After floods in this river, waste from this mine lay over a fairly large area of farmland all along the shore of this river.
This mine started to produce in 1951. And because there are floods every spring, damages caused to farmland along the river by cyanide as well as by other chemical products used in the working of the mine have turned those lands to waste. Farmers wronged in their rights as owners have made representations without obtaining any damages, because
Criminal Code
the laws then in force did not permit to find out clearly where the responsibility lay.
Last fall I travelled a distance of 60 miles down the Laflamme river to its junction with the Bell river and, over more than half that distance, I saw deposited along the river mine waste which surely destroyed a large part of the vegetation as well as all the fish in many places that, formerly, were a great attraction for tourists and people of that area. Even farther north, an area quite good for moose hunting has also been affected.
Following this damage, needless to say, it will be many years before normal conditions are restored, despite the fact that, since then, the mine has gone out of business owing to financial difficulties.
However, the farmers from Rochebeau-court, whose farms have been damaged cannot claim any more for the losses they have sustained since the mine in question is practically bankrupt.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I think it would be proper to act without any delay. I therefore support the motion introduced by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson) and I suggest:
-that the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing a measure to provide appropriate punishment for the offense of water pollution.

The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Is there a contract or agreement in effect between the government and the Bell Telephone Company with respect to the Bell Telephone Company operating the telephone system of the various government departments and agencies?
2.	If so, how much was paid to the Bell Telephone Company for the fiscal years 1956-57 and 1957-58?
3.	What formula, if any, is used for determining the amounts to be paid to the Bell Telephone Company?
Question
Answer by: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
1.	Yes.
2.	The Bell Telephone Company was paid the following amounts for switchboard and local telephone service in Ottawa:
1956- 57	 $1,115,342.00
1957- 58	 1,221,312.00
3.	The standard tariffs for telephone exchange service as fixed by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and specific services provided under terms of the agreement concluded between the government and the Bell Telephone Company.

Tuesday, June 10, 1958
